opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where the field has actually learned a lot in the last couple of years.

The way I like to think about it is that the residual stream is kind of the communication bus of the model. It's this shared space that every layer reads from and writes to, and so it's where you'd expect to find the model's working representations: the concepts it's carrying forward, the intermediate conclusions it's building up. That's why a lot of the early sparse autoencoder work focused there. If you want to know what the model is "thinking about" at a given point, the residual stream is the natural place to look.

But the MLPs and attention are doing really different jobs, and I think tools should respect that rather than treating everything as one undifferentiated pile of activations. Attention is fundamentally about moving information between positions. It's answering "which earlier tokens matter for this one, and what should I copy over from them?" So interpretability for attention naturally needs to be relational. You care about the query-key structure, which heads attend where, and what gets written through the OV circuit. Looking at a single position's activation in isolation misses a lot of what's going on.

MLPs, on the other hand, act position-wise. They're more like the place where the model does lookups and computation: recalling facts, applying transformations, sharpening features. There you tend to want something like transcoders, where you're trying to explain the MLP's output in terms of its input, so you get an actual account of the computation and not just a description of the state.

And I think that distinction is the important one. Describing a state versus describing a computation. If you only decompose the residual stream, you get a nice dictionary of features, but you don't necessarily learn how one feature leads to another. The more recent circuit-tracing and attribution-graph style work is exciting precisely because it tries to stitch these together, using things like cross-layer transcoders for the MLP side and then tracing how information flows through attention, so you can follow a computation end to end.

The practical upshot for anyone building tools is to pick the decomposition that matches the question. If you're doing monitoring or steering and you want to know whether a concept is present, residual stream features are often great. If you want to understand why the model produced an output, you need to account for the mechanisms that actually move and transform information, and that means treating attention and MLPs as distinct kinds of operations.

r001.rationale: The response says sparse autoencoders have been used on the residual stream and that residual features can be useful, but it does not identify them as a likely solution for interpreting the residual stream.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest starting point is that these three components are doing fundamentally different kinds of work, and a lot of early interpretability treated them too uniformly.

The residual stream is the shared workspace. Every layer reads from it and writes back into it, so whatever representation you find there is a superposition of contributions from everything upstream. That's why it's such a natural target for things like sparse autoencoders and probing. You're sampling the model's "state of belief" at a given depth. But the flip side is that the residual stream doesn't compute anything on its own. If you only study it, you get a sequence of snapshots without the mechanism that moved you from one to the next.

MLPs are where a lot of the actual nonlinear computation lives. They act on each token position independently, so they're best thought of as something like a lookup or a feature transformation. If you want to understand factual recall, or how the model combines a few features into a new one, that's typically an MLP story. The tooling needs to respect that locality. You shouldn't expect an MLP neuron to "know" about other positions, and if your explanation requires that, you've probably misattributed something.

Attention is the only place information moves across positions. So the right questions there are routing questions. Where is information being pulled from, under what conditions, and what gets written when it arrives? Attention heads have that useful QK and OV decomposition, where you can separate "who to attend to" from "what to copy," and tools that exploit that structure tend to be more interpretable than ones that just look at attention patterns as heatmaps.

So practically, I'd say: use the residual stream to ask what the model represents, use MLPs to ask how features get transformed, and use attention to ask how information gets moved. And the real win comes when you connect them into circuits, because the interesting behaviors almost never live in just one component. An attention head moves something into position, an MLP acts on it, and the result lands back in the residual stream for the next layer to read. If your tool only sees one of those, it'll give you a story that's locally correct but globally incomplete.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be careful about treating those as interchangeable places to apply the same tool. They play different roles in the computation, so the questions you ask should be different.

The residual stream is this shared space where information accumulates. Looking at it can help you understand what information is available at a particular point in the model. But finding information there doesn’t necessarily tell you how it got there, or whether the model actually uses it.

With MLPs, you’re asking more about transformations: what patterns does this component respond to, and what does it write back into the residual stream? With attention, you also have to account for how information moves between positions. And an attention map alone isn’t the full explanation, because you need to understand what information is being moved and what the receiving position does with it.

So I’d want tools that respect those differences but let you connect them. Can you follow a piece of information from where it’s produced, through where it’s routed, to where it affects the output? And then can you intervene on that proposed pathway and see whether the model behaves as you’d predict? That’s the step from an interesting visualization toward an explanation of the computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be careful about treating those as interchangeable objects. The residual stream is this shared representation that different parts of the model read from and write to. So if you find a feature there, that tells you something about what information is available, but it doesn't necessarily tell you which computation produced it or how it's being used.

With MLPs, you're asking more about transformations: what patterns does this component respond to, and what does it write back? With attention, you also have to account for relationships between token positions. Where is information being moved from, and what determines that routing?

So I wouldn't expect one visualization or one decomposition to answer all of those questions equally well. You want tools that respect the structure of each component, but that also let you connect them. Can you follow a piece of information from an earlier token, through an attention head, into the residual stream, and then see how an MLP changes it? And ultimately, can you intervene on that proposed mechanism and show that it actually affects the behavior you're trying to explain? That's what turns an interesting description into a stronger explanation.
